title: Ancient Lebanese city of Tyre added to heritage danger list
description: Tyre, an ancient Phoenician city in southern Lebanon bombarded by Israel over recent months, was added Tuesday to the UNESCO list of world heritage sites in danger. The ancient city, founded some 4,700 years ago, is home to two protected sites listed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites, a Roman triumphal arch and a hippodrome dating from the second century.

title: UNESCO places ancient Lebanese city of Tyre on heritage danger list
description: UNESCO on Wednesday added Tyre, an ancient coastal city in southern Lebanon founded by the Phoenicians, to its list of world heritage sites in danger following months of Israeli bombardment. Founded around 4,700 years ago, Tyre is home to archaeological treasures including two protected UNESCO areas.

title: Ancient ferns turned Triassic Europe into a wildfire inferno
description: Ancient fern savannahs may have transformed parts of Europe into a wildfire-prone inferno during the end-Triassic mass extinction. New fossil evidence suggests the ferns repeatedly regrew after fires, creating fresh fuel that helped prolong the devastation.

title: Sokasi At Four Seasons Resort Bali At Sayan Is A Culinary Tribute To Bali’s Ancient Recipes
description: To the rhythmic lapping of the sacred Ayung River and a clear starlight sky, I seat myself at Sokasi at Four Seasons Resort Bali at Sayan. My interactive dining experience is a delicious Balinese vegetarian meal thoughtfully tailored by Head Chef Suta (Wayan Sutariawan), a celebrated cookbook author. The experience is rooted in Sokasi’s signature Chef’s Table experience that, through seven courses, explores forgotten recipes and beloved classics passed down through generations. Drawing on guests’ preferences and dietary requirements, each menu is adapted, creating a personal journey through Bali’s rich culinary traditions. Head Chef Suta Bamboo has woven itself into Bali’s social fabric, be it in daily life or during ceremonies. At Sokasi, bamboo is omnipresent – from the sustainable design of the riverside restaurant to its cooking utensils, rice steamers, sate sticks, and even its cooking techniques. Even its name, Sokasi, refers to a bamboo-woven basket. The Dining Experience Sokasi The restaurant has a leaf-shaped design, an open kitchen, and a stone counter where I am seated. Chef Suta is ready and starts the meal with Timbungan Jamur, a dish usually prepared in certain areas on religious holidays. Delightfully, I watch the chef scoop out wild mushrooms marinated in spices from Timbungan, or from the bamboo segment in which they have just been cooked. A local sour fruit, a fresh salad of herbs from the resort’s garden, and coconut further enhance the flavour and aroma of the dish. Timbungan Jamur As I relish each spoonful, Chef Suta gets hands-on with preparing the next dish – baby corn with its husk gets chargrilled and basted with sambal merah, which is a tomato and chilli relish. Base Gede literally translates to ‘big/complete spice’ and is a fundamental spice paste of various fresh and dry ingredients that add their aromatic magic to Balinese cooking. I nod in approval as Base Gede, with a garnish of a crunchy spiced peanut mixture, completes my second course. Chargrilled Baby Corn As Chef peppers the meal with anecdotes about his life growing up in a village in East Bali, the enjoyable fine-dining experience also provides an interesting glimpse into the age-old culinary traditions of Bali. “The flavours and recipes that I grew up with are often only found in Balinese family homes today, and it is a privilege to share these traditions through Sokasi,” adds Chef Suta, for whom cooking is both a source of joy and a way to connect guests with the heritage, craftsmanship, and sense of place that define Bali's rich food culture. The generational recipe of Kalio Jamur involves tender pumpkin being cooked with spices in a curry. As I savour mine, the lemongrass sauce is creamy, the addition of galangal makes it aromatic, and the slight heat from chilli adds to the overall flavour of the traditional dish. Klengis Kelor, the fourth course dish, is a forgotten village delicacy whose star ingredient is Klengis, which is the wholesome leftover coconut pulp after coconut oil is extracted. It has become rare to make Klengis from scratch as it is a labour-intensive process, making it a ‘lost’ recipe. “At Four Seasons Resort Bali at Sayan, we champion zero waste. Our Klengis is made by simmering grated coconut flesh with water for two hours; the oil at the top is skimmed off while the remaining strained pulp or Klengis is used to make the gluten-free Klengis Kelor,” explains Chef Suta . For the plant-based dish, moringa leaves marinated in Klengis are wrapped in corn husk, chargrilled, and topped with tomato salsa. Freshly picked Kemangi or lemon basil from the resort’s herb garden adds the zingy flavour to the dish . My broad, satisfied smile after polishing the plate clean is a clear indication of my joy at eating the nutrient-dense, delicious dish. Chef Kuta tells me that in Bali, moringa leaves are consumed not just for their health benefits, but also because they are considered to spiritually cleanse by averting negative energy. Amidst the anticipation of the next dish, the Tempe Merangi arrives, where a sauce prepared with raw shallots, chilli, lime, and tomatoes is lavishly spread over Tempe to give it a citrusy flavour. I am reminded of my maiden attempt to cook Tempe at Jala Cooking Academy in Four Seasons Resort Bali at Jimbaran Bay. A few days ago, I had happily wrapped seasoned Tempe in a banana leaf, secured the ends with bamboo pins, and steamed the wrap before savouring it at Jala. My multi-course lunch, during which I donned the chef's hat for the afternoon, is a culinary memory I regularly return to. My next course contains coconut, but this time it is burnt to give a smoky flavour to the dish. Cauliflower, which has been marinated with garlic and coconut sauce, is grilled on a wood fire and served with burnt coconut sauce, lemongrass, red chilli, and ginger. The delectable explosion of flavours in my mouth as I bite into the perfectly marinated smoky cauliflower instantly makes me look appreciatively at the chef. The last course is my favourite since I have a massive sweet tooth. I am in gourmand heaven when Jamu Kunyit arrives. Coconut sorbet, tamarind caviar, turmeric foam, and orange tuile irresistibly call out to me. “This dessert is my interpretation of a traditional medicinal drink known as Jamu Kunyit Asam. Made with Kunyit, which is fresh turmeric, and Asam, which is tamarind, this herbal drink dates back to the 8th century. It’s Bali’s wellness brew,” explains Chef Suta. It’s the perfect way to complete my visually appealing, soul-satisfying Balinese vegetarian seven-course meal.
